joke.title: The knocking lettuce

lines.de: Was ist grün und klopft an die Tür?
lines.en: What is green and knocks on the door?
A 'knock lettuce'.

breakdown.en: made-up word: klopfen (to knock) + der Salat (lettuce)

joke.explain:
The pun: [[der Kopfsalat]] is a real word, 'head lettuce', the normal round lettuce you buy. Add one letter and **Kopf** (head) becomes **Klopf** (knock).

'Was ist grün und ...?' (What is green and ...?) is a classic pattern of German children's jokes. You will meet more of them.

fact.title: A glove is a hand shoe

lines.de: Ein Handschuh ist ein Schuh für die Hand.
lines.en: A glove is a shoe for the hand.

fact.explain:
German builds new words by gluing plain words together, and read literally they are often funny:

- [[die Glühbirne]] (light bulb) = glow pear
- [[die Schildkröte]] (turtle) = shield toad
- [[das Stinktier]] (skunk) = stink animal
- [[das Faultier]] (sloth) = lazy animal
- [[der Kühlschrank]] (fridge) = cool cupboard

The last part decides the article: [[der Schuh]], so [[der Handschuh]].

phrase.title: Passt schon.

lines.en: It's fine. / Don't worry about it.

breakdown.note: passen = to fit; the 'es' (it) is dropped

breakdown.en: already; here it softens: 'it's fine, really'

phrase.explain:
Very Bavarian, and you will hear it in Munich many times a day: when you apologise for bumping into someone, when you are a few cents short at the bakery, when you ask 'Is that OK?'. It means 'it's fine, no problem'.

The full sentence is [[Das passt schon.]], but people drop [[das]]. Even shorter: [[Passt!]] = OK, deal.

joke.title: Pirates and circles

lines.de: Warum können Seeräuber keine Kreise berechnen?
lines.en: Why can't sea robbers calculate circles?
Because they guess pi.

breakdown.note: sends the verb to the end: weil sie Pi raten

joke.explain:
Say the punchline aloud: 'Pi raten' sounds exactly like [[Piraten]] (pirates). And to calculate a circle you need π, so if you only guess it ...

Notice [[weil]]: after it, the verb goes to the end ([[weil sie Pi raten]]). That comes at A2; for now just notice it.

fact.title: The yes that English doesn't have

lines.en: Aren't you hungry? - Yes, I am!

fact.explain:
German has a special 'yes'. When someone asks a **negative** question or says something negative and you disagree, **ja** is confusing and **doch** is the answer:

- [[Hast du keinen Hunger?]] - [[Doch!]] (Yes, I am hungry!)
- [[Das ist nicht teuer.]] - [[Doch!]] (Yes, it is!)

French has 'si' for this; English and Russian have no single word. You will also hear [[doch]] as a softener: [[Komm doch mit!]] = Come along, why don't you!

phrase.title: Na, alles klar?

lines.en: Hey, how's it going? / All good?

phrase.explain:
A casual greeting between friends and colleagues, literally 'Well, everything clear?'. It isn't really asking whether you understood. Answer [[Ja, alles klar. Und bei dir?]] (Yes, all good. And you?).

In shops and bars, [[Alles klar!]] also means 'OK, got it'.

joke.title: The shortest German joke

lines.en: Two hunters meet.
Both dead.

joke.explain:
Often called the shortest German joke. [[sich treffen]] means 'to meet', but [[treffen]] also means 'to hit a target'. 'Treffen sich zwei ...' is how many German jokes start (like 'Two guys walk into a bar'), so you expect a meeting. The punchline switches to the other meaning: they hit each other.

The verb comes first here. That is normal at the start of jokes and stories: [[Kommt ein Mann zum Arzt ...]] (A man goes to the doctor ...).

fact.title: ß got a capital letter

lines.de: Seit 2017 gibt es auch ein großes ß: ẞ.
lines.en: Since 2017 there has also been a capital ß: ẞ.

breakdown.note: very common: Es gibt keine Milch. = There's no milk.

fact.explain:
For centuries ß was the only German letter without a capital form, so words in capitals used SS: STRASSE. Since 29 June 2017 the capital ẞ is part of the official spelling ([[STRAẞE]]), and SS is still correct too.

It matters for names in passports: Weiß and Weiss are different family names. You won't type ẞ often, but now you know what it is.

phrase.title: Stimmt so.

lines.en: That comes to 18.40 euros.
Keep the change.

phrase.explain:
How Germans tip. In a café or restaurant the waiter tells you the total at the table. You hand over a note and say [[Stimmt so.]] (literally 'it's right like this'), which means 'keep the change'.

Or you name the amount you want to pay, tip included: [[Zwanzig, bitte.]] or [[Machen Sie zwanzig.]] (Make it twenty.) Around 5-10% is normal.

joke.title: A cookie in the shade

lines.de: Was ist ein Keks unter einem Baum?
lines.en: What is a cookie under a tree?
A shady little spot. (Or: a shady cookie.)

breakdown.note: der Baum; einem after unter (dative, Unit 6)

breakdown.en: 1) a nice little spot  2) a Christmas biscuit

joke.explain:
[[Plätzchen]] has two meanings: a little place ([[der Platz]] + -chen) and a small biscuit, especially the ones Germans bake before Christmas. 'Ein schattiges Plätzchen' is a common phrase for a nice spot in the shade, so a cookie in the shade is ... a shady Plätzchen.

And -chen makes it das, as always.

fact.title: Munich means 'at the monks'

lines.en: 'München' actually means 'at the monks'.

fact.explain:
The name comes from Old High German 'munichen', 'at the monks', after a settlement of monks where the old town is now. That's why the city's coat of arms shows a figure in a monk's robe, the [[Münchner Kindl]] (Munich child).

Over the centuries the monk got younger and cuter. On souvenirs today it's a child in a hooded robe, often holding a beer mug and a radish. Look for it on city signs.

phrase.title: Mahlzeit!

lines.en: (the lunchtime greeting at work, roughly 'Enjoy your lunch!')

breakdown.note: das Mahl (meal, an old word) + die Zeit (time)

phrase.explain:
Walk through a German office around lunchtime and colleagues greet each other with [[Mahlzeit!]] instead of [[Hallo]]. It's short for 'Gesegnete Mahlzeit' (blessed meal). The answer is simply [[Mahlzeit!]] back.

Some people find it old-fashioned or funny, but it's everywhere in offices, canteens and workshops, so it's a real work phrase for you.

joke.title: The boomerang

lines.de: Wie nennt man einen Bumerang, der nicht zurückkommt?
lines.en: What do you call a boomerang that doesn't come back?
A stick.

breakdown.note: zurückkommen = to come back; the verb goes to the end

joke.explain:
No pun this time, just dry logic, which Germans love.

Two useful things: [[Wie nennt man das auf Deutsch?]] (What do you call that in German?) is a great question for class. And [[man]] means 'people, you in general': [[Man sagt ...]] = People say ...

fact.title: Oktoberfest starts in September

lines.en: Oktoberfest starts in September.

breakdown.note: im = in dem; months take im

fact.explain:
Most of the Oktoberfest happens in September. It starts on a Saturday in the second half of September and ends on the first Sunday in October, or on 3 October if that is later. The reason is better weather.

Munich people call it [[die Wiesn]], after the Theresienwiese (Therese's meadow) where it takes place. The first one, in 1810, was the wedding party of Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese.

phrase.title: Zusammen oder getrennt?

lines.en: Together or separately? (paying the bill)

phrase.explain:
When a group asks for the bill ([[Zahlen, bitte!]] or [[Die Rechnung, bitte!]]), the waiter asks this. Splitting the bill is completely normal in Germany, even on a date.

Answer [[Zusammen, bitte.]] (one bill) or [[Getrennt, bitte.]] (each pays their own). Then each person says what they had: [[Ich hatte den Kaffee und die Breze.]]

joke.title: Waiter, there's a fly ...

lines.de: Herr Ober, da ist eine Fliege in meiner Suppe!
lines.en: Waiter, there's a fly in my soup!

lines.de: Keine Sorge, die isst nicht viel.
lines.en: Don't worry, it doesn't eat much.

breakdown.note: an old-fashioned way to call a waiter
die Suppe; meiner after in (dative, Unit 6)

joke.explain:
'Herr Ober, ...' jokes are a whole genre, the German version of 'Waiter, there's a fly in my soup'.

Two useful bits: [[Keine Sorge!]] (Don't worry!) is everyday German. And [[die]] here means 'it': Germans often point at something with der/die/das instead of er/sie/es.

Nobody says 'Herr Ober' in real life any more. Call a waiter with [[Entschuldigung!]]

fact.title: Gift is poison

lines.en: 'Gift' is not a present.

fact.explain:
Watch out for false friends, words that look English but aren't:

- [[das Gift]] = poison (a present is [[das Geschenk]])
- [[der Chef]] = boss (a cook is [[der Koch]])
- [[bekommen]] = to get, not 'become': [[Ich bekomme ein Bier.]] = I'll have a beer.
- [[der Rat]] = advice, council (a rat is [[die Ratte]])
- [[also]] = so, therefore ('also' is [[auch]])

phrase.title: Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?

lines.en: Can I pay by card?

breakdown.note: können: ich kann; question, so the verb comes first
with kann, the second verb goes to the end

phrase.explain:
Germany still likes cash more than most countries. Some small bakeries, kiosks and beer gardens take cash only; the sign says [[Nur Barzahlung]] or [[Nur bar]]. So it's worth asking before you order.

Answers: [[Ja, klar.]] or [[Nur bar, leider.]] (Cash only, sorry.)

Unit 3 preview: with [[kann]], the second verb goes to the end: [[Ich kann mit Karte zahlen.]]

joke.title: The hiking fruit

lines.de: Was ist orange und wandert durch die Berge?
lines.en: What is orange and hikes through the mountains?
A 'hikerine'.

breakdown.note: durch = through; der Berg, die Berge

breakdown.en: made-up word: wandern + die Mandarine (mandarin orange)

joke.explain:
The pun: [[die Mandarine]] + [[wandern]] (to hike).

[[wandern]] is a national hobby, especially in Bavaria, with the Alps about an hour from Munich. It's also a false friend: it means hiking, not wandering around. You'll hear [[Wir gehen am Wochenende wandern.]] (We're going hiking at the weekend.)

fact.title: A 63-letter word

lines.de: Ein Gesetz hatte einen Namen mit 63 Buchstaben.
lines.en: A law had a name with 63 letters.

fact.explain:
The law was the [[Rindfleischetikettierungsüberwachungsaufgabenübertragungsgesetz]] of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a 'beef labelling supervision duties delegation law'. It was repealed in 2013, and the word went with it.

Read it in parts, from the end:

- Gesetz = law
- Übertragung = transfer, delegation
- Aufgaben = duties
- Überwachung = supervision
- Etikettierung = labelling
- Rindfleisch = beef (Rind = cattle, Fleisch = meat)

That is how to read any long German word: split it up. The last part is the main word and decides the article: [[das Gesetz]].

phrase.title: Ich schau nur.

lines.en: Can I help you?
Thanks, I'm just looking.

breakdown.note: schauen = to look; spoken without the -e

phrase.explain:
What to say when a shop assistant comes over.

In speech, Germans often drop the -e of the ich form: [[ich schau]], [[ich hab]], [[ich geh]]. In writing it's [[ich schaue]]. [[schauen]] is the southern word; in the north you'll also hear [[gucken]]. A longer version: [[Ich schaue mich nur um.]] (I'm just looking around.)

joke.title: Five animals from Africa

lines.de: Die Lehrerin fragt: 'Fritzchen, nenn mir fünf Tiere aus Afrika!'
lines.en: The teacher asks: 'Fritzchen, name five animals from Africa!'
Fritzchen: 'Three lions and two elephants!'

breakdown.note: nennen; the du command (Unit 5); mir = to me

joke.explain:
Fritzchen is the cheeky schoolboy of German jokes, like 'Little Johnny' in English. His jokes almost always start in class with a teacher's question.

Good plural practice: [[der Löwe]] - [[die Löwen]], [[der Elefant]] - [[die Elefanten]].

fact.title: One bread roll, many names

lines.de: In München sagt man Semmel, nicht Brötchen.
lines.en: In Munich people say Semmel, not Brötchen (bread roll).

breakdown.note: the verb comes second, after In München

fact.explain:
The bread roll has a different name almost everywhere:

- [[das Brötchen]] (standard German, north and west)
- [[die Semmel]] (Bavaria, Austria)
- [[die Schrippe]] (Berlin)
- [[das Weckle]] (Swabia)
- [[das Rundstück]] (Hamburg)

In a Munich bakery, ask for [[zwei Semmeln, bitte]] and [[eine Breze]] (a pretzel; Breze in Bavaria, Brezel elsewhere). Nobody minds Brötchen, but Semmel sounds local.

phrase.title: Brauchen Sie den Kassenbon?

lines.en: Do you need the receipt?

breakdown.note: polite; yes/no question, so the verb comes first
der Kassenbon: die Kasse (till) + der Bon (slip); den: accusative (Unit 4)

phrase.explain:
The cashier's standard question at the supermarket or bakery. Answer [[Nein, danke.]] or [[Ja, bitte.]]

Other words for a receipt: [[der Bon]], [[der Beleg]], and [[die Quittung]] (a proper receipt, e.g. for work expenses).

More checkout questions: [[Brauchen Sie eine Tüte?]] (Do you need a bag?) and [[Mit Karte oder bar?]] (Card or cash?)

joke.title: White and annoying

lines.de: Was ist weiß und stört beim Essen?
lines.en: What is white and bothers you while you eat?
An avalanche.

breakdown.note: beim = bei dem; das Essen = eating, food

joke.explain:
Pure absurd humour, another 'Was ist ... und ...?' classic.

Useful from it: [[Störe ich?]] (Am I disturbing you?), and the hotel door sign [[Bitte nicht stören]] (Do not disturb). [[beim Essen]] = while eating; also [[beim Arbeiten]] = while working.

fact.title: 'Handy' is a German word

lines.de: Das Handy ist ein deutsches Wort.
lines.en: 'Handy' is a German word.

fact.explain:
It looks English, but no English speaker calls a phone a 'handy'. German has many such fake English words:

- [[das Handy]] = mobile phone
- [[der Beamer]] = projector (in English, a 'Beamer' is a BMW)
- [[das Public Viewing]] = watching football together on big screens (in English: viewing a body before a funeral)
- [[der Oldtimer]] = vintage car
- [[der Smoking]] = tuxedo

Meanwhile English borrowed real German words: kindergarten, angst, rucksack, wanderlust, zeitgeist.

phrase.title: Schönen Feierabend!

lines.en: Have a nice evening! (said when work ends)

phrase.explain:
[[der Feierabend]] is the moment work ends and your own time begins, and Germans take it seriously. Say [[Schönen Feierabend!]] to colleagues when one of you leaves work. The answer is [[Danke, dir auch!]] or, formally, [[Danke, Ihnen auch!]]

Also: [[Ich habe Feierabend.]] (I'm done for the day.) and [[das Feierabendbier]] (the after-work beer). The phrase is short for [[Ich wünsche dir einen schönen Feierabend.]]

joke.title: A clown at the office

lines.de: Was macht ein Clown im Büro?
lines.en: What does a clown do at the office?
Faxes. (Faxen also means 'fooling around'.)

joke.explain:
[[faxen]] is 'to send a fax', and [[die Faxen]] are silly antics: [[Faxen machen]] = to clown around. Germany is also famous for still using fax machines in offices and doctors' practices, which makes the joke a little truer there.

Handy phrase: [[Lass die Faxen!]] = Stop fooling around!

fact.title: Germans press their thumbs

lines.en: I'll keep my fingers crossed for you!

fact.explain:
Germans don't cross their fingers for luck, they press their thumbs: fold each thumb inside your fist and squeeze. Before an exam or a job interview, a colleague will say [[Ich drücke dir die Daumen!]]

Polite form: [[Ich drücke Ihnen die Daumen.]] The answer is just [[Danke!]]

phrase.title: Ist hier noch frei?

lines.en: Excuse me, is this seat free?
Sure!

breakdown.note: yes/no question: the verb comes first

phrase.explain:
In beer gardens, canteens and on trains, strangers share tables and benches. Before you sit down, ask [[Ist hier noch frei?]] (literally 'Is here still free?').

If the seat is taken: [[Nein, leider besetzt.]] (No, sorry, it's taken.) You can also ask about a chair: [[Ist der Platz noch frei?]]
